title: Ischemic colitis: watershed rectosigmoid junction after hypotension
vignette: A 72-year-old man develops mild abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea after undergoing urgent cholecystectomy. The surgery was complicated by an episode of hypotension that was treated with bolus intravenous crystalloid fluids. The patient had no previous gastrointestinal bleeding. His last colonoscopy 10 years ago was normal. Past medical history is notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a myocardial infarction 7 years ago. The patient smoked for 40 years and quit after the myocardial infarction. Colonoscopy would most likely show pathology in which of the following portions of the large bowel?

clues.text: mild abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea
clues.note: Crampy abdominal pain with bloody diarrhea after a hypotensive event is the classic presentation of ischemic colitis.

clues.text: complicated by an episode of hypotension
clues.note: A hypotensive (low-flow) episode is the trigger for nonocclusive colonic ischemia, which strikes the poorly perfused watershed zones first.
Diabetes and atherosclerosis (also HTN, prior MI, smoking) create underlying arterial insufficiency, making watershed areas vulnerable during hypotension.
Established atherosclerotic disease (prior MI, smoking) predisposes to marginal perfusion, so a drop in pressure tips watershed colon into ischemia.

whatMatters: Bloody diarrhea + abdominal pain after a hypotensive (low-flow) episode in a vasculopath = nonocclusive ISCHEMIC COLITIS. Ischemia hits the watershed zones between major arterial supplies - the splenic flexure (SMA/IMA border) and the RECTOSIGMOID JUNCTION (IMA/superior rectal border). Among the choices, the rectosigmoid junction is the watershed area. Answer D.
strategy: Recall the colonic watershed zones: splenic flexure (between SMA and IMA) and rectosigmoid junction (between the last sigmoid branches of the IMA and the superior rectal artery). In low-flow states these marginal areas ischemia first. Of the listed segments, only the rectosigmoid junction is a watershed; the cecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure, and mid-transverse colon are well perfused by SMA branches.

eliminations.label: Ascending colon - well perfused by SMA
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: proximal colon supplied by the ileocolic/right colic branches of the SMA. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is not a watershed zone, so it is relatively protected in low-flow states. ✅ Correct if: SMA embolism/occlusion (acute mesenteric ischemia of the small bowel/right colon).

eliminations.label: Cecum - SMA territory, not watershed (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the cecum, supplied by the ileocolic artery (SMA). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it lies within a single robust arterial territory, not at an SMA/IMA border, so it is not the first to ischemia in hypotension. ✅ Correct if: SMA occlusion or cecal volvulus.

eliminations.label: Hepatic flexure - SMA supply
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the right colic/middle colic (SMA) supply region. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is not a classic watershed area (the watershed is the SPLENIC flexure, at the SMA/IMA junction). ✅ Correct if: the question offered splenic flexure.

eliminations.label: Mid-transverse colon - central SMA territory
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: mid-transverse colon supplied by the middle colic artery (SMA). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is well perfused, unlike the SMA/IMA watershed at the splenic flexure. ✅ Correct if: middle colic artery occlusion.

reasoning: Bloody diarrhea + pain after hypotension in a vasculopath = nonocclusive ischemic colitis
Low-flow ischemia targets watershed zones between major arterial supplies
Colonic watersheds: splenic flexure (SMA/IMA) and rectosigmoid junction (IMA/superior rectal)
-> rectosigmoid junction is the listed watershed; answer D
mechanism: The colon is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (SMA; proximal to the splenic flexure) and the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA; distal colon), connected by the marginal artery of Drummond; the distal rectum also receives supply from the internal iliac artery (via the superior rectal from IMA). Two 'watershed' zones lie between adjacent arterial territories and receive the most tenuous perfusion: the SPLENIC FLEXURE (SMA-IMA border) and the RECTOSIGMOID JUNCTION (between the last sigmoid branches of the IMA and the superior rectal artery). In nonocclusive low-flow states - here systemic hypotension during surgery in a patient with diabetes and atherosclerosis - these marginal zones become ischemic first, producing ischemic colitis (crampy pain, bloody diarrhea; colonoscopy shows pale mucosa with petechial hemorrhages). The well-vascularized cecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure, and mid-transverse colon (all SMA territory) are relatively spared, and the rectum has collateral rectal-artery supply. Of the options given, the rectosigmoid junction is the vulnerable watershed.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid GI > colonic watershed areas: splenic flexure (SMA/IMA) and rectosigmoid junction (IMA/superior rectal); ischemic colitis in low-flow states; marginal artery of Drummond.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Post-hypotension bloody diarrhea = nonocclusive ischemic colitis at a watershed - pick the rectosigmoid junction among the choices.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on watershed area, SMA vs IMA territory, marginal artery of Drummond, or nonocclusive ischemia? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Cecum/ascending/hepatic flexure/mid-transverse are all SMA territory (well perfused); only the rectosigmoid junction (with splenic flexure) is a watershed.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: ischemic colitis watersheds = splenic flexure + rectosigmoid junction; low-flow -> pale mucosa + petechiae on colonoscopy.
